description: Hola, soy Ingeniero Industrial enfocado en análisis de datos, estadística con Python/SQL y desarrollo web frontend. Mi proyecto aborda el reto "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!", creando una herramienta interactiva para detectar, graficar y validar matemáticamente tendencias ambientales con datos abiertos de la NASA.
summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web application designed to identify, visualize, and statistically validate long-term environmental changes across our planet using open NASA Earth science datasets (including NASA POWER and Giovanni).
Because a single global climate driver can produce opposite trends in different regions, selecting the right indicators and proving whether a shift is real or mere natural variability is a major challenge. Our tool solves this by letting users explore 26 years of historical time series (2000–2025) for key variables like precipitation, surface temperature, and humidity. Through side-by-side regional comparisons, the app calculates the annual rate of change using Sen’s Slope estimator and applies the non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test to determine statistical significance.
This tool empowers researchers, students, and decision-makers to rapidly distinguish true climate trends from seasonal noise and understand how interconnected Earth systems behave across contrasting geographies.
details:
What it does and how it works
Earth System Trend Detective — Mexico is an interactive 3D geospatial and statistical analytics web application designed to uncover, visualize, and scientifically validate long-term environmental changes across contrasting regions of Mexico using 26 years of NASA Earth science data (2000–2025).

Users select key environmental indicators—such as 2-meter air temperature (T2M), bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), and relative humidity (RH2M)—and compare contrasting Mexican climate zones (such as the Arid North vs. the Tropical Southeast or Central Mexico). An interactive year-by-year timeline slider (2000–2025) dynamically updates a 3D orbital globe with broadcast-style thermal wave halos, regional teleconnection arcs, and dynamic time-series curves. Beneath the visualizations, an automated statistical engine computes the annual rate of change using Sen’s Slope Estimator and evaluates statistical significance (p < 0.05) via the non-parametric Mann-Kendall Trend Test.

Benefits and intended impact
Because a single global climate driver can produce opposite trends in neighboring regions, separating true climate shifts from natural seasonal variability is difficult. Our tool translates complex NASA datasets into clear visual and statistical evidence, helping students, researchers, urban planners, and local communities quickly understand what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the shift is scientifically significant.

Tools, coding languages, and software used

  • Data Sources: NASA Giovanni and NASA POWER (26-year monthly historical records from January 2000 to December 2025).
  • Programming Language & Framework: Python and Streamlit (with custom space-themed CSS).
  • Data Processing & Statistical Analysis: Pandas, NumPy, and pymannkendall (Mann-Kendall test and Sen’s Slope).
  • 3D & Interactive Visualization: Plotly (Scattergeo orthographic 3D projection and dynamic time-series charts).
  • Development & Deployment: GitHub Codespaces, GitHub, and Streamlit Community Cloud.

Creativity and key factors considered
Instead of static tables, we designed an intuitive "weather-broadcast meets orbital control room" interface featuring dynamic heatwave halos that expand and shift color as users scrub through decades, paired with year-by-year narrative summaries ("Detective Chronicles"). Key factors considered included handling missing satellite values (-999), choosing non-parametric statistical methods robust against climate outliers, and highlighting regional teleconnections across diverse Mexican biomes.
